analysis.one_liner: Requires cosmetics makers to register with the FDA, disclose ingredients, report injuries, and gives the FDA power to order recalls of unsafe products.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support from 16 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Cosmetics are nearly unregulated at the federal level: companies do not have to register with the FDA, list every ingredient with regulators, or report when a product seriously injures someone, and the FDA cannot force a recall of a dangerous shampoo or hair dye. This bill would require facility registration and ingredient disclosures (with fees for larger companies), annual FDA safety reviews of at least five ingredients, mandatory reporting of serious injuries, and authority to order recalls and halt sales of unsafe products. Small makers under $500,000 in sales would be mostly exempt. It was introduced by Senator Dianne Feinstein with Republican Senator Susan Collins and referred to the Senate Health Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses makeup, shampoo, lotion, hair dye, or deodorant — nearly all Americans — plus salon workers, who are exposed to these chemicals at far higher levels than consumers. Today the FDA cannot order a recall of a dangerous cosmetic, companies face no federal requirement to register or disclose formulas, and there is no mandatory reporting of serious injuries like chemical burns, infections, or hair loss. The bill also targets specific known hazards for the first round of safety reviews, including lead acetate (a hair dye ingredient) and formaldehyde-related chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday cosmetics users and salon workers

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA mandatory recall authority over cosmetics likely to cause serious harm, after first giving the company a chance to recall voluntarily [S3].
Requires companies with over $2 million in annual cosmetic sales to pay registration fees, with the money earmarked only for cosmetics safety work [S3].
Requires companies to report serious injuries — deaths, hospitalizations, disfigurement, significant hair loss — to the FDA within 15 business days [S3].

Orders the FDA to begin safety reviews of five named ingredients in the first year, including lead acetate and formaldehyde-related chemicals, and at least five ingredients per year thereafter, with authority to set concentration limits and warning labels [S3].
Exempts small makers with under $500,000 in annual sales from registration entirely and gives reduced requirements to companies under $2 million in sales [S3].
Directs the FDA to encourage alternatives to animal testing and to share data to avoid duplicate animal tests [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large cosmetics companies pay registration fees scaled to sales and bear the cost of filing ingredient statements, safety attestations, injury reports, and eventual manufacturing standards. Consumers might see small price increases. States give up some power to set their own stricter cosmetics rules going forward.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large cosmetics manufacturers, plus state regulators

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state rules: once the FDA starts reviewing an ingredient, states are barred from imposing new requirements on it for over a year, and states are fully preempted on registration, manufacturing standards, recalls, and injury reporting [S3]. A state with stricter standards could not add new protections beyond what the federal order requires.
The review pace is slow: the FDA must complete only five ingredients per year, while cosmetics contain thousands of ingredients, so most would go unreviewed for decades [S3].

Companies largely vouch for their own products: a manufacturer's safety determination is presumed adequate if it cites an expert body's statement or its own testing, and the FDA only demands records when it has specific reason to suspect harm [S3].

Companies between $500,000 and $2 million in annual sales — small businesses by most standards — still face registration, annual ingredient statements, and safety attestations, a real compliance burden for tiny brands [S3].

The FDA's cosmetics safety program would be funded by industry fees rather than general taxpayer appropriations, and the bill limits the FDA's authority to act against ingredients that cause only minor, transient reactions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: it would give the FDA tools over cosmetics it has lacked since 1938 — recall power, injury reporting, and ingredient reviews of known hazards like lead acetate. The costs fall mainly on large manufacturers, which are best positioned to absorb them, and the bill goes out of its way to shield small makers. The biggest honest objections are structural: the five-ingredients-per-year pace means most ingredients would never be reviewed, and the preemption section trades away states' ability to move faster than the FDA. On balance a consumer would be better protected under this bill than under current law, but it is a modest step, not a comprehensive overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee the day it was introduced in May 2017, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on May 11, 2017, joined from the start by Republican Senator Susan Collins [S1].

It attracted 16 cosponsors — 13 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it [S4,S5].
No version of the bill ever received a vote in either chamber, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics manufacturers came out ahead: they continue to operate under 1938-era rules with no federal facility registration, no ingredient disclosures to the FDA, no requirement to report serious injuries, and no mandatory recall authority.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — a Democratic lead sponsor, a Republican lead co-sponsor, and 16 cosponsors split 13 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the bill never advanced past referral, so no vote ever revealed how the full chambers leaned [S4,S5].

industries.industry: Large cosmetics manufacturers (brands over $2 million in annual sales)
industries.note: The bill charges them registration fees scaled to sales and imposes ingredient disclosures, injury reporting, safety attestations, and eventual manufacturing standards — new costs under rules the industry has avoided since 1938. But it also preempts stricter future state laws and gives them a single national standard to follow instead of a patchwork, and it largely lets them vouch for their own product safety [S3].

The bill requires fragrance and flavor suppliers to give the FDA the complete ingredient lists of their blends on request within 30 days — information they currently treat as trade secrets. Consumers benefit because hidden allergens and sensitizers in fragrance mixtures become traceable by regulators [S3].

industries.industry: Small cosmetics makers (under $2 million in sales)
industries.note: Makers under $500,000 in sales are exempt from registration and fees entirely, and companies under $2 million get extended deadlines, simplified safety paths, and no annual injury report requirement. Those between $500,000 and $2 million still carry registration, ingredient statement, and attestation duties, which is a genuine burden for tiny brands [S3].

Salons are excluded from facility registration, and products meant only for professionals must carry warning labels and list all ingredients — protections for workers who handle concentrated products daily [S3].
